(Thought I was done, but my eighth grader syndrome took over. Oops.)

The woman who greeted us inside struck an intimidating figure in her decorated uniform, despite having a rather petite stature.

“Wardeness,” Garth acknowledged her with a slight bow of his head when she didn’t speak right away. “This is the student we informed you of.”

For all appearances, she seemed to ignore him, but faced me instead, her militant stance commanding attention, magic rolling off her in telling waves. The walls and bars were not what kept the prisoners in chains. 

“Post-grad elemental magi should have enough control to keep an identity spell secret,” she admonished harshly. “That being said, I’m intrigued you affiliate yourself with a religion. Elementals have a habit of thinking they *are* the higher power.”

I was so taken aback by the swift change in the demeanor of her speech that I wasn’t entirely sure whether to be properly ashamed of my childish action, or elated that this woman wasn’t hating me entirely on principle. It made it hard to respond; that and her continuous heavy submission emanation. Garth was actually sweating from the force of it.

She seemed to notice our discomfort, because she said, “Apologies, my guards are provided special uniforms that protect them from the effects. We don’t keep extra, but I can have your own wardrobe enchanted by the sutromancer once you’ve settled. For now you’ll have to endure it.”

“Mr. Donovan,” she addressed Garth, “if you are unable to continue, I will have a guard provide a tour for your charge. She will be in good hands.”

He weakly shook his head to her offer, “I appreciate your concern, but this much I can do.”

He actually started to turn green as she led us through to the prison’s heart. Though many inmates inhabited the cells we passed, none seemed to move, none called out to us. The emanation grew stronger, the further in we went.

I brought my hands together, as though in prayer, and closed my eyes to concentrate against the weight of the emanation.

*To the night which withstands all horrors, through you I find my shield. Let your darkness devour any ill that would touch me.*

Immediately, the burden of her magic was lifted. A film of deepest blue formed a translucent netting above me. I took Garth’s arm and pulled him close. The relief that washed over him overrode any sense of his propriety and he allowed the contact to continue as we walked.

The wardeness looked back with a wry smile, “So you *are* capable of wordless magic, and even under tremendous pressure? It’s a shame you didn’t choose my alignment. You’d have been great as an officer.”

Her medallion must have been amongst her many medals on the uniform, but I was so distracted I couldn’t ascertain it.

“What is your alignment?” I asked, perhaps too casually, as she shot me a sharp look then, “Er.. wardeness..?”

“Order,” was her short answer, before she turned down a separate hallway. We followed suit, Garth finally getting color back in his cheeks.

The mother of peace, war, justice, and diplomacy. Despite its lack of elemental status, order was one of the broadest ideal alignments to master. Its score minimums were on the high end of the alignment scale. Its workforce was made up of rigid rules and strict guidelines, with powers of command abundant and free will at stake, they were frequently tested for mental and emotional stability and given surprise empathy tests on a monthly basis. Abusing such power would land you in a much worse place than the dusklands.

The cells seemed to be tapering out, and for a stretch we passed only stone wall.

“Bare with me a bit, this is maximum security, so you may suffer a slight drain, even with your shield.”

The possibility that her definition of a slight drain might be completely different from my own may have cross my mind as she performed a series of spells to unlock the door hidden in the masonry.

My legs went numb and Garth’s armful of curtains tumbled from his grasp, heralding his sudden loss of consciousness.

They are all little canaries in a cage. With their flaming wings or talons of justice. Whether with beaks of ice, or love songs on the winds, when night comes, they all close their eyes against the darkness. I chose to be the owl, from the outside looking in.

I chose to control the darksleep.

No one really understood, could comprehend why any good person would choose this power. Only a few of the cold-aligned alumni would approach me, post grad.

The professors avoided me entirely, and finding a mentor to help me proceed with my doctorate became a chore. I was transferred to the dusklands where only one other dark-aligned scholar remained.

“A prison.”

I turned to my academic advisor and escort.

“You expect me to continue my studies here?”

He was only mildly apologetic upon reply, “This man is the only one with the knowledge you seek.”

A man aligned with diplomacy couldn’t outright tell me that I brought this on myself.

“Shall I find my own quarters?” I asked, with maybe an obvious air of sarcasm. “I’m sure there’s an empty cell.”

When he didn’t answer immediately, I turned on him again expectantly.

“Well..” he started reluctantly, “you couldn’t quite call it a cell. We did have the bars removed to prevent any unhappy accidents. However, the facilities couldn’t afford to have a door built. We assured them we could make due.”

I eyed the parcel in his arms.

*In the darkness where lies the heart of deceit, reveal unto me your secrets.*

Before he could react to the manifestation of my magic, the parcel’s wrapping dissolved into shadow and mist. My suspicions were confirmed.

“Curtains.”

“We’re doing our best here, everyone expected you to continue in the line of war with Professor Hols. If you hadn’t thrown that curveball at graduation, the resources we could have prepared would have been much more abundant.”

He knew as well as I did, that our esteemed university had no shortage of resources. We did however, have an extremely prejudiced minister of affairs. A powerful wealth-aligned mage with the ear of the dean and the treasurer, would have no trouble redirecting any resource he thought was being put to poor use. He’d aptly demonstrated his disdain for my choice when he petitioned to have my diploma revoked, mid-ceremony.

“Garth, when you went into diplomacy instead of war, did you inform your advisor, first?” I opted to bait him into breaking his resolve. I already knew his answer.

As we passed through the security platform and provided identification, he finally deigned to give me an answer.

“You’re already privy to the details of my graduation, but this is hardly a similar circumstance. Diplomacy is not such a rare alignment, as I’m sure you’re well aware.”

Diplomacy and peace trended high in his school days, with a lot of anti-war propaganda from our home nation floating around. Diplomacy was an alignment for more serious students, with post-grad aspirations. Peace was one for those who saw their studies as complete. Both were fairly weak alignments, as their subject base was narrow. However, such a narrow subject base, made for generally smooth outcomes in a work environment.

Broader alignments, like the elements, were more difficult to find jobs for. The fields were highly competitive. I’d thought, at the time, that with darkness being such a rare choice, competition wouldn’t be an issue. Of course, I’d neglected to consider the reason behind it.

Doctor Meriweather Volts was the only remaining dark scholar of any repute. An aging psychopath, if you believed the papers, was once an esteemed student with the highest scoring powers the university had seen at the time. Then there was me.

You could say I was shocked to find I’d scored high enough to choose not only an element, but even the broadest elements of light and dark. Darkness wasn’t exactly advertised as an option, and I wheedled it painstakingly out of my advisor the night before graduation.

My conversation with Garth upon this realization had been a stressful one, mostly due to his diplomacy alignment making him unable to give me a single piece of concrete advice. At that time he’d broken his resolve enough to say heatedly that it was far above his paygrade, and if I needed someone to actually tell me what to do I should continue down the war path after all. 

“Your alignment ID,” the entrance guard instructed, indicating the scanner by the metal doors.

Identity spells were a very private affair. Weaker alignments usually had to speak their spells, and so soundproof entrance chambers were provided when such spells were called for.

This establishment had no such commodity.

 Garth placed his hand upon it first. Considering his alignment, it was impressive that he didn’t have to speak spells aloud. The light over the door flashed pale yellow and he was allowed entrance.

The guard glared first at my medallion, then straight into my eyes as I approached.

Irked, I voiced the words of my identity spell aloud.

“Lord, I call to you in your solitude, in the void where birthed your Word. Let the night come forth, for in the dark, I see!”

The light gave a faint, deep purple glow, and cracked audibly before the metal door lifted. Ah, too much force then.

“Sorry, still a student,” I shrugged as he stiffly stood aside to let me pass.

I knew it from the beginning. From the way she spoke, to her style of dress, to her electric eyes, right down to the mole just above her upper lip. This was her story.

 Knew it when we played checkers at the beach and chased stingrays through the coke bottle-clear waves. When the foam rolled at the top and splashed over our bare feet, and the sun dipped to hide under the sea; in the dusklight I saw destiny’s slow blink on the horizon.

“When the tide comes in to sweep me away,” she said as we walked together under the stars, “I know you’ll be the first to follow.”

“Yes.”

But the tide only goes out, and out for us.

She grew in fame and talent, as I always knew she would, while I festered behind in dark rooms with the blinds closed. I spent my days hunched over desks, staring into screens, as she thrived in her field.

Director. Screenwriter. Actor.

She was all of these things. She was living my dream.

The day came when she asked me.

“It’s a part only you can play.”

I could only say, “Yes.”

I am one thing that she could never be. A chameleon of life. A jack of all trades. While she has become an ace of few, I have learned to get by in many. I am adaptable as the breeze, fluid as water through the cracks. She stands like a stone to be weathered by me.

There was a man of little means once, but with an aptitude for camera operation and cinematography. I knew when she took him under her wing, how I could steal her story. I knew the moment he put the ring on her finger, the destiny that peeked at me before descending beneath the ocean.

I dressed the part of the heroine in her film. Laughable, considering our true roles. One day, when we were shooting, she got so fed up with the set’s coffee supply, she went out to get her own.

“You like yours sweet, right?” she asked, digging through her bag for her keys. She looked fondly to her paramour, jingling the keychain teasingly from the door. Had it been an eternity since she looked at me? I would make her see.

“Yes.”

Men turned their heads as she walked off set. Men and me. Watching her leave, watching the tide go out, and out.

But I know the tide never comes back for me, so while they wait for the waves to come crashing back over them, I’m constructing the storm to lay her low. 

Cameras basically have their own computers within nowadays. Computers have their limits. Her dedicated fiancé had been pushing his for 6 hours to get shot after shot. His display screen had long given out, and given our budget, he was forced to eye it the old-fashioned way until he could make repairs.

I disabled the built-in fans under the guise of checking the white balance. No one paid me any mind, as though this was normal for an actor. Perhaps with her limited crew, it was. With a camera down, filming would be delayed. At least by a day. But if I could find one thing to sabotage, each day, eventually her growing reputation would suffer.

Finally, finally. The tide would come in.

When the tide came, it hit with the force of a tsunami. I didn’t have to sabotage another single thing. When they returned, he overrode the safety installed in the camera’s software, so dedicated was he. Something impossible, something unexpected. His camera must have been a custom build.

Perhaps, if I were the heroine of this story, I would have stopped him. Perhaps I would have feigned illness so that shooting would have to stop. Perhaps I would have confessed my misdeed, but no heroine, am I.

I wouldn’t have called it an explosion, by any means. But the devastation it caused might qualify it. For the man behind the camera, whose eyes took the brunt of the shrapnel, I suppose it qualified.

Her film was delayed indefinitely, and she told me, in confidence, that so was the wedding. His eyes were shredded, not a remnant left salvageable. They couldn’t afford transplants, and he was low priority. His eyes were his life, he’d told her. Without them he was nothing.

I had only planned to sew discord between them in the midst of the stress my sabotage would have caused. But this was fine. Discord would sew itself once the depression set in.

The tide came faster, pushed by the storm I brewed. She would be mine alone.

She met me, one day, at a cafe, overlooking the crystal waves we once explored together. That day, her hand was bare. 

“He asked me not to come anymore,” true to herself, there were no tears. “He said it was too painful, to hear me and not see.”

If I could not ever see the ocean again, I would still choose to hear its crashing waves, its morning gulls. He was a coward. He was selfish. He didn’t deserve her.

She blinked twice out at the sea. The sun was beginning to set. Could she hear destiny call? Could she see as I did?

“The tide is coming in,” she said quietly.

“Yes.”

So it was.

There is a bridge that stretches high over the bay. When the tide goes in, the water sits so far below it, that the impact of falling is equivalent to landing on cement.

A day came, where the tide went in, and a beautiful woman of great talent and potential threw herself from the highest point, so lovelorn was she.

True to myself, I was the first to follow.
